query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing near-equiatomic Al into FeCoNi to form a FeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy with partial B2 ordering will increase its coercivity above that of FeCoNi-based soft ferromagnets (e.g., FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt).
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic FeCoNi alloy with established soft ferromagnetic properties.
generation.intervention: Incorporate ~25 at.% Al, melt under vacuum in an arc furnace, homogenize at 1000–1200 °C, and quench to promote partial B2 ordering.
generation.conditions: Maintain overall composition near equiatomic to achieve a configurational entropy ≥ 1.0R. Control the homogenization temperature and rapid cooling to retain partial B2 order.
generation.structural_mediator: B2-ordered domains distributed within the FeCoNiAl matrix, acting as domain-wall pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: Partial B2 ordering enhances local atomic ordering and increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy, impeding domain-wall motion and raising coercivity while largely preserving saturation magnetization.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coercivity at least twice that of FeCoNi (or FeCoNiPd/FeCoNiPt) baselines, maintaining reasonably high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: Soft-ferromagnetic FeCoNi derivatives (e.g., FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt) with low coercivity and high saturation magnetization.
generation.boundary: Al composition must remain near ~25 at.% and the alloy processed to preserve single-phase behavior and partial B2 order; insufficient ordering or off-stoichiometry could negate coercivity gains.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of the B2 region and its thermal stability remain uncertain; mechanical property changes arising from partial B2 ordering are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Arc-melt and homogenize Fe25Co25Ni25Al25, verifying partial B2 phase via X-ray diffraction and TEM while measuring coercivity under the same conditions as baseline FeCoNi-derived alloys.
measurements: XRD for phase determination and degree of B2 ordering
Transmission electron microscopy to observe B2 domains
Vibrating sample magnetometry or VSM-based hysteresis loops at room temperature for coercivity and saturation magnetization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured coercivity does not exceed the baseline FeCoNi-based alloys by at least ~2× under identical measurement conditions, or if no partial B2 ordering is found in the alloy, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

The saturation magnetization (MS) and coercivity (Hc) for the four different samples analyzed in the present study have been listed in Table 1. The MS of AlCoFeNi is substantially higher compared to that of the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy for both heat-treated conditions. While the magnetization is primarily determined by composition and the crystal structure, the coercivity can be affected by impurities, deformation, grain size and phase decomposition. The coercivity (Hc) decreased with increasing annealing temperature from 15 Oe for sample aged at 600 °C/15 h, exhibiting nanoscale phase separation, to 4 Oe for samples aged at 1000 °C/15 h, exhibiting a homogeneous undecomposed B2 matrix. A similar observation has been reported in the literature, where the coercivity of the AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA annealed at 1000 °C/2 h decreases by 30 Oe (from 45 Oe to 15 Oe) compared to as-cast alloys. The AlCoFeNi HEA investigated in the present study exhibits higher saturation magnetization and lower coercivity than other soft ferrite magnetic materials, e.g., MnZn ferrite, Cu-Zn-Ti ferrite,, as revealed in Supplementary Table 2.

occupying_moves.lever: Introduce Al to form a near-equiatomic FeCoNiAl alloy (partial B2 ordering)
occupying_moves.technique: Conventional arc melting followed by homogenization heat treatment
occupying_moves.conditions: Synthesis with ~25 at% of Fe, Co, Ni, and Al each; solution-annealing near 1000–1200°C, then quenching

chosen.lever: Partial B2-forming Al addition to FeCoNi for equiatomic configuration
chosen.technique: Arc melting with controlled stoichiometry, homogenization at high temperature, water quench
chosen.conditions: Target Fe25Co25Ni25Al25 composition, T ~1000–1200°C, hold for hours, rapid cooling
chosen.why: Because FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt remain soft ferromagnets, adding Al in an equiatomic ratio increases configurational entropy above 1.0R while also promoting partial B2 ordering that enhances domain-wall pinning. This raises coercivity relative to FeCoNi-based soft magnets. Prior studies of Fe–Co–Al alloys show that B2-type structural ordering can strengthen magnetic anisotropy, suggesting that the Al-driven ordering in an equiatomic FeCoNiAl matrix will provide greater coercivity. This can be tested by measuring hysteresis loops under the same conditions as the baseline alloys: if no coercivity increase (at least >2× over the baseline) is observed, then the hypothesis of B2-order-driven domain-wall pinning—and thus the predicted higher coercivity—would be falsified.
